title: The Diesel cycle: heat added at constant pressure and the cutoff ratio
examples: What is the difference between the Otto and Diesel cycles?
Why are diesel engines more efficient?

explain.say: Lorries, ships and generators mostly run on diesel. Rudolf Diesel patented his engine in 1892 with a clever twist: no spark plug. He squeezed air so hard that it became hot enough to light the fuel the moment it was sprayed in. Look at the cylinder: an injector where the spark plug would be.

draw.text: The Diesel cycle: heat added at constant pressure and the cutoff ratio

explain.say: The cycle starts like Otto's, but squeezes harder: a compression ratio of 18, from 0.9 litres to 0.05. The pressure climbs to about 5700 kilopascals and the air gets hot enough to ignite diesel. See the steep rise on the left? Now the fuel is sprayed in gradually. What happens to the pressure while it burns?

It stays flat! The piston moves down while the fuel burns, so heat is added at constant pressure. Injection stops at the cutoff, here when the volume has doubled: a cutoff ratio of 2. Then the gas expands adiabatically. See the flat top of the loop? Why might a longer cutoff give more power?

More fuel burns per cycle, but efficiency drops. The efficiency formula has the Otto term times a cutoff correction: about 63.2 percent here. Now compare: an Otto cycle at the same ratio of 18 would be 68.5 percent, more! See the bars? So why are diesel engines more efficient in real life?

Because a petrol engine cannot reach 18 without knocking; it is stuck near 10, at about 60 percent. The diesel only compresses air, so it can go much higher. Excellent! Real link: big marine diesels reach above 50 percent real efficiency, among the best engines ever built. Exam tip: at equal compression ratio, Otto beats Diesel.

draw.text: Same r: Otto wins. Real engines: Diesel wins via higher r

faq.q: How does a diesel engine ignite its fuel?
faq.a: It compresses air so much that its temperature rises above the fuel's self-ignition point. The injector sprays fuel into this hot air and it lights on its own, with no spark.
The ratio of the cylinder volume when fuel injection stops to the volume at the start of injection. A larger cutoff ratio means more fuel burned per cycle but lower efficiency.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Otto and Diesel cycles?
faq.a: Otto adds heat at constant volume, after a spark; Diesel adds heat at constant pressure, as fuel is injected into hot compressed air. For the same compression ratio, Otto is more efficient.

faq.q: Why are diesel engines more efficient?
faq.a: They can use much higher compression ratios, about 15 to 22, because only air is compressed, so there is no knock. The higher ratio more than makes up for the constant-pressure heat addition.

facts: Rudolf Diesel patented his compression-ignition engine in 1892.
For the same compression ratio, the air-standard Otto cycle is more efficient than the Diesel cycle.
